name: single-table-inheritance
intent: Map an inheritance hierarchy of classes onto one shared table whose columns are the union of all classes' fields, using a type code (discriminator) column to decide which class each row instantiates, so polymorphic reads need no joins.
problem: A class hierarchy must be persisted, the hierarchy is small and its classes share most fields, and cross-class queries or polymorphic loads are frequent: mapping each class to its own table would force a join per level on almost every read, while the subtypes differ by only a few columns.
context: Object-relational mapping of a small, shallow, stable class hierarchy whose subclasses are mostly variations on shared state - domain-model inheritance (Employee/Engineer/Manager), payment or content types - where the storage layer is chosen by the team and the persistence framework can be taught the type code (JPA/EF Core/ActiveRecord/SQLAlchemy/most ORMs make this their default strategy) or the mapping is written by hand over SQL.
benefits: No joins: a polymorphic read or write touching shared and subtype fields is one row of one table, which is the documented motivation for the pattern - it minimises the joins that mount up when a hierarchy is spread over several tables.
One identity space and one place for the shared columns: a row is an object, foreign keys and indexes pointing at the hierarchy stay simple, and class-table joins disappear from every query path.
Cheap new subtypes: a new subclass is new (mostly nullable) columns plus a new class/mapper entry, not a new table, a new join path or a backfill of existing rows.

Uniform tool support: STI is usually the framework default (JPA SINGLE_TABLE, EF Core table-per-hierarchy, Rails' type column, SQLAlchemy polymorphic_on), so the mapping is declared in metadata instead of hand-written mappers.
Whole-hierarchy queries and reporting stay simple: one table with a type column answers both 'all employees' and 'all engineers' with a filter, no set operations across tables.
tradeoffs: The table is sparse and keeps widening: every subtype adds nullable columns, and the database cannot express NOT NULL for a subtype's fields, so subtype invariants move from the schema into code (frameworks make derived columns nullable by definition).

Cross-subtype coupling: unrelated subtypes share one table's constraints, indexes, locks and DDL footprint, and a schema change for one subtype rewrites the definition for all of them on the hot table.

Discriminator rot: the class <-> type-code mapping is duplicated knowledge that the database does not enforce, and an unmapped value surfaces as a runtime mapping failure (EF Core throws on a discriminator absent from the model; ORMs cannot instantiate an unknown class).
Wasted I/O and no per-subtype loading: rows carry columns irrelevant to their type, so wide rows cost page reads, and lazy loading cannot avoid subtype fields that live in the same row.
Evolution and exit cost: splitting the table later (to class-table inheritance) is a data migration over live data, and dropping a subtype leaves its columns and its old discriminator values behind.

participants.responsibility: Declares the shared state and the polymorphic interface of the hierarchy; it owns no table of its own, only the shared columns.
Adds subtype-specific state and behaviour; its fields become extra nullable columns of the same table, and it maps its own type-code value.
Column holding the value that names the class of a row; the single piece of data that lets a mapper decide which class to instantiate.
Reads and writes rows for one class: filters by its discriminator, maps shared and subtype columns, and creates instances of that class only.
Holds the union of all classes' fields plus the discriminator; enforces what the schema can (shared NOT NULLs, keys, CHECKs) and leaves subtype invariants to the mapper.

use_cases: Small stable hierarchies where subclasses share most state: Employee/Engineer/Manager, Payment/CardPayment/WirePayment, Notification/EmailNotification/PushNotification.
Content or asset models with a handful of similar types (Photo/Question/Post, Blog/RssBlog) distinguished by a type code, where cross-type queries and listings are the dominant read.
Legacy or third-party schemas that already hold a hierarchy in one table with a kind column and must be mapped onto domain classes without restructuring the database.
Reporting and analytics over a hierarchy where one wide table with a type column beats joining four tables for every subtype question.

ORM-default configurations: teams that pick the framework's default hierarchy mapping (JPA SINGLE_TABLE, EF Core TPH) because join avoidance and mapping simplicity outweigh column honesty for their hierarchy size.

Rails Active Record single-table inheritance: ActiveRecord::Inheritance stores the subclass name in the table's type column by default (Company/Firm/Client all live in companies with type = 'Firm'), so fetching via the base class returns correctly-typed objects - GitLab runs a production monolith on this mechanism and maintains a written policy on when STI must not be used.

EF Core's default table-per-hierarchy mapping: a Blog/RssBlog hierarchy shares one table, the discriminator's name, CLR type and per-class values are set with HasDiscriminator/HasValue, and EF Core automatically adds the discriminator predicate to derived-type queries (throwing on unmapped discriminator values).

SQLAlchemy declarative polymorphic mappers: the base class declares polymorphic_on = 'type' in __mapper_args__ and each subclass a unique polymorphic_identity, so one person table answers polymorphic queries for Person/Employee rows without joins.
avoid_when: The hierarchy is large or still growing: the table becomes a sparse union of unrelated attributes and every read pays for columns of other subtypes - use class-table inheritance (one table per class, joined on the key).

Subtype fields need real schema guarantees (NOT NULL, unique, foreign keys, per-subtype indexes): a single table cannot express them - use class-table inheritance, or concrete table inheritance when duplication is acceptable.

The 'subtypes' are really independent entities that happen to share a few columns: sharing one table couples their lifecycles and migrations - use composition plus a mapped superclass/embeddable rather than polymorphic storage.
Weights differ per subtype (one class is huge, others are rare rows): the wide table penalises the common case - consider class-table inheritance or splitting the heavy subtype into its own table.
A key-value/JSON document store is already the target: serialized LOB or a document column expresses the same 'one row, different shapes' idea without a type code the database cannot police.
anti_patterns: Using STI as a dumping ground: adding 'just two more nullable columns' for every new kind until the table is a union of unrelated concepts whose rows are 80% NULL.
Storing the type code but deciding behaviour with scattered switch/instanceof checks in domain code instead of mapping to polymorphic classes or keeping the decision inside the mapper.
Letting the type code drift from the class model (renaming a class, renumbering values, hand-written INSERTs) so that production rows become unloadable or silently materialise as the wrong type.
Wrapping a legacy wide table in an ORM hierarchy without cleaning the data: nullable-column rot and 'unknown discriminator' exceptions appear only under load in production.

Assuming the framework default is STI where it is not (Sequelize documents concrete-table inheritance; Django's multi-table inheritance joins per parent), so the intended storage strategy silently changes.
design_principles: Representational gap: the schema is not the object model, so the mapping knowledge (which columns belong to which class, which discriminator value means which class) belongs in the mapper/metadata layer, not scattered through domain code.
Single source of truth for the discriminator: one declared value per concrete class, written by exactly one place (the mapper or the ORM metadata) and never renumbered.
Open/closed: new subtypes arrive as new classes with nullable columns, so the existing mapping and queries stay unchanged for existing types.

Keep the schema honest where it still can be: shared columns NOT NULL, keys and CHECK constraints on the type code, and an explicit migration to class-table inheritance once subtype invariants matter more than join avoidance.
YAGNI on schema precision: for a small, stable hierarchy the join tax of class-table inheritance is paid on every read, while the column waste of one table is paid only in storage.
best_practices: Declare the discriminator explicitly (column name, type and one value per class) rather than relying on a framework default, so the values are reviewable and stable across refactors and providers.
Write the discriminator from one place (the mapper or ORM metadata) and treat 'unknown discriminator' as a hard error with a log line naming the table and value, never as an empty object.
Keep the hierarchy shallow and shared columns dominant: measure the table's width and NULL density before adding the next subtype, and record the decision.
Index the discriminator when single-subtype queries are common, and let the ORM add its subtype predicate (EF Core and JPA do this automatically) instead of hand-rolling type filters in queries.
Enforce what the database can: NOT NULL on shared columns and CHECK constraints for 'column X is required exactly for type Y' on small tables, so the most damaging drift fails at write time.

Plan the exit: when subtype-specific NOT NULL/FK guarantees or independent write volume become requirements, migrate to class-table inheritance and keep the mapper shape stable (Inheritance Mappers), doing it as an explicit data migration.
sources: Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (Addison-Wesley, 2002) - Single Table Inheritance, Chapter 12 Object-Relational Structural Patterns.
